Let $G$ be a graph on $n$ vertices such that at least $n/2$ vertices have degree at least $n/2$. Must $G$ contain every tree on at most $n/2$ vertices?
#580: [EFLS95]
graph theory
A conjecture of Erdős, Füredi, Loebl, and Sós. Ajtai, Komlós, and Szemerédi [AKS95] proved an asymptotic version, where at least $(1+\epsilon)n/2$ vertices have degree at least $(1+\epsilon)n/2$ (and $n$ is sufficiently large depending on $\epsilon$).
Zhao [Zh11] has proved this conjecture holds for all sufficiently large $n$. 
Komlós and Sós conjectured the generalisation that if at least $n/2$ vertices have degree at least $k$ then $G$ contains any tree with $k$ vertices.
See also the entry in the graphs problem collection.

 Update to my submitted proof claim:
A complete and citable manuscript presenting the certified finite verification is now available:
Certified SAT Verification of the Vertex Formulation of Erdős Problem #580 for Orders at Most 19
The paper proves the literal vertex formulation of Problem #580 for every integer n with 1 <= n <= 19. The principal new computer-assisted case is n = 18. An edge-minimal hypothetical counterexample is first reduced to a specific bipartite structure. Of the 47 non-isomorphic trees on nine vertices, 42 are handled by theoretical embedding results, while the remaining five exceptional trees reduce to four rooted-core configurations. The corresponding SAT instances are then certified to be unsatisfiable using complete CNF files and DRUP proof certificates.
The manuscript substantially strengthens the documentation and auditability of the result. It includes an independent second-solver verification, reverse-unit-propagation checking of the certificates, a standalone semantic reconstruction of every clause, reproducible generation of the complete table of 47 trees, and byte-for-byte regeneration of all four published CNF instances.
The paper should be read together with the associated computational archive:
Zenodo repository containing the SAT instances, DRUP certificates, verification scripts, audit tables, and reproducibility materials
This new paper provides an expanded, citable, and independently auditable presentation of the previously submitted finite verification. It strengthens the mathematical exposition, certification, and reproducibility of the contribution, while the verified range remains 1 <= n <= 19.

A partial proof 
claimed by Rafik Zeraoulia (using OpenAI GPT-5.6 Thinking).
 Summary:
 I claim a computer-assisted verification of the literal vertex formulation of Erdős Problem #580 for every $n\leq 19$.
For $n=18$, an edge-minimal counterexample reduces to a graph partitioned into sets $L$ and $S$ of size $9$, with every vertex of $L$ having degree $9$ and $S$ independent. Known special cases reduce the $47$ trees on nine vertices to four marked rooted-core configurations. A Hall-type extension argument and four SAT encodings, all proved UNSAT by CaDiCaL, exclude every reduced counterexample. The case $n=19$ follows by deleting one high-degree vertex. This does not cover the stronger classical edge formulation.
